ecg-cond-014.question: A 74-year-old woman presents with presyncope. What is the diagnosis on this tracing?
commentaires: Correct: a pause with no P wave whose duration is not a multiple of the PP interval: failure of sinus node automaticity.
Incorrect: the pause (≈ 3.2 s) is not an exact multiple of the baseline PP interval (≈ 860 ms), as type II SA block would require.
Incorrect: no premature P wave deforms the T wave preceding the pause.
Incorrect: AV block requires a P wave not followed by a QRS; here, no P wave appears during the pause.
ecg-cond-014.explication: On this tracing, sinus rhythm (about 70 bpm) is abruptly interrupted by a pause of about 3.2 s with no P waves at all. The absence of P waves during the pause indicates a failure of atrial activity rather than an AV conduction disorder: this is therefore not AV block, which would show a P wave not followed by a QRS. A pause that is not an exact multiple of the PP interval points to sinus arrest (failure of automaticity) rather than type II sinoatrial block, in which the pause equals exactly 2 (or n) PP intervals. A blocked PAC is recognised by a premature P wave, often hidden in the T wave preceding the pause. A symptomatic pause > 3 s warrants discussion of pacing.
ecg-cond-014.aRetenir: Pause with no P wave, not a multiple of PP = sinus arrest; pause of exactly 2 PP = type II SA block.

ecg-cond-015.question: A 68-year-old man reports "skipped beats". Analyse the pause on this tracing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
commentaires: Incorrect: sinus arrest produces a pause with no arithmetical relationship to the PP interval; here it equals exactly two cycles.
Incorrect: Mobitz I would show a non-conducted P wave after PR prolongation; here, there is no P wave during the pause.
Incorrect: respiratory arrhythmia makes the PP interval vary gradually and cyclically, without an abrupt 2-cycle pause.
Correct: the pause equals exactly 2 PP intervals (≈ 1600 ms for a PP of 800 ms): the sinus impulse failed to exit to the atrium.
ecg-cond-015.explication: On this tracing, the baseline PP interval is about 800 ms (75 bpm) and the pause, with no P wave, measures exactly two cycles (1600 ms): the sinus impulse was generated but failed to exit to the atrium. This is type II second-degree sinoatrial block (sinoatrial Mobitz II). Sinus node activity itself is not visible on the surface ECG; the block is inferred from this arithmetical relationship. Sinus arrest would produce a pause that is not a multiple of the PP interval. Mobitz I AV block would show a non-conducted P wave. Respiratory arrhythmia produces gradual, cyclical variations without an abrupt pause.
ecg-cond-015.aRetenir: Type II second-degree SA block: pause equal to an exact multiple of the baseline PP cycle.

ecg-cond-016.question: A Holter recording repeatedly shows progressive shortening of the PP intervals, followed by a pause with no P wave lasting less than two PP intervals. The PR interval is constant. What is the most likely mechanism?
commentaires: Correct: shortening PP intervals followed by a pause < 2 PP: this is Wenckebach at the sinoatrial junction.
Incorrect: type II SA block produces a pause equal to 2 PP, with no preceding shortening of the PP intervals.
Incorrect: sinus arrest does not reproduce this repetitive sequence of shortening PP intervals before the pause.
Incorrect: constant PR and no non-conducted P wave: the block is not atrioventricular.
ecg-cond-016.explication: Type I SA block reproduces Wenckebach periodicity at the sinoatrial junction: sinoatrial conduction time lengthens progressively, with decreasing increments, which shortens successive PP intervals until an impulse is blocked. The pause is then less than 2 PP. The constant PR interval and absence of a non-conducted P wave rule out Mobitz I AV block. Type II SA block would produce a pause equal to 2 PP without preceding shortening. Sinus arrest does not show this repetitive sequence. This is an indirect surface diagnosis with no specific therapeutic implication: correlation with symptoms guides the decision.
ecg-cond-016.aRetenir: Type I SA block: shortening PP intervals then a pause < 2 PP, like Wenckebach at atrial level.

ecg-cond-017.question: Faced with a pause during sinus rhythm, what sign should you look for to suggest a blocked premature atrial contraction rather than a sinus pause?
ecg-cond-017.reponseAttendue: A premature P wave, often hidden in the T wave preceding the pause and deforming it (a T wave that is more peaked, notched or taller than the other T waves).
ecg-cond-017.explication: A very early PAC arrives while the AV node is still refractory: it is not conducted, and it resets the sinus node, hence a pause. Its P wave is often hidden in the preceding T wave, which it deforms (peaked, notched or taller than the others). This is the first benign cause of a "pause" to exclude, by carefully comparing all the T waves. A pause equal to two PP intervals would rather suggest type II SA block, and progressive PR prolongation AV Wenckebach. Blocked PACs in bigeminy can mimic severe sinus bradycardia.
ecg-cond-017.aRetenir: Before calling it a sinus pause, look for a premature P wave hidden in the T wave.

ecg-cond-018.question: A 45-year-old woman reports occasional "ectopic beats". What is the diagnosis on this tracing?
commentaires: Incorrect: a PVC would be broad, with a different morphology and no premature P wave before it.
Incorrect: the abnormal cycles are premature beats; the modest pause that follows is not a sinus pause.
Incorrect: no P wave is blocked; every P wave is followed by a QRS.
Correct: premature beats with an identical narrow QRS, preceded by a P wave whose morphology differs from the sinus P.
ecg-cond-018.explication: On this tracing, a few premature narrow-QRS beats are preceded by a P wave whose morphology differs from the sinus P wave. A premature beat preceded by an abnormal P wave (morphology or axis different from the sinus P wave) with a narrow QRS identical to the baseline QRS is a premature atrial contraction. The pause that follows is usually non-compensatory, because the PAC resets the sinus node. A PVC would produce a broad QRS without a premature P wave. Mobitz II manifests as a blocked sinus P wave, not a premature beat. A PAC conducted with aberration may, however, have a broad QRS: the premature P wave remains the key.
ecg-cond-018.aRetenir: Premature beat + different P wave + narrow QRS = premature atrial contraction.

ecg-cond-019.question: A 76-year-old woman with known paroxysmal AF has syncope during Holter monitoring: abrupt termination of an AF episode followed by a 5 s pause before the first sinus beat. What is the diagnosis?
commentaires: Correct: a post-conversion pause after an AF episode, the typical form of sick sinus syndrome.
Incorrect: no non-conducted P wave is described; the pause is sinus, not atrioventricular.
Incorrect: there is no prodrome or trigger, and the pause immediately follows termination of the AF episode.
Incorrect: there is no triggering by head rotation or neck pressure.
ecg-cond-019.explication: A post-conversion pause after an AF episode reflects an abnormally long sinus node recovery time: this is the typical form of tachycardia–bradycardia syndrome, a manifestation of sick sinus syndrome (sinus node dysfunction). The mechanism is suppression of sinus node automaticity by the tachycardia (overdrive suppression). This is not AV block, since no non-conducted P wave is visible. The context fits neither typical vasovagal syncope (prodrome, trigger) nor carotid sinus hypersensitivity (triggered by head rotation). The documented symptom–rhythm correlation here is ideal.
ecg-cond-019.aRetenir: Pause on termination of AF = tachycardia–bradycardia syndrome.

ecg-cond-020.question: In the same patient (tachycardia–bradycardia syndrome with syncope due to a post-conversion pause), which approach is consistent with the 2021 ESC guidelines?
options: Observation alone, since post-conversion pauses are by nature transient
Implantable defibrillator for prevention of sudden cardiac death
Uptitration of the beta-blocker to prevent AF episodes
Cardiac pacing, or AF ablation in a selected patient
commentaires: Incorrect: syncope due to a documented pause requires action; recurrence is common and may cause injury.
Incorrect: no ventricular arrhythmia is involved; there is no indication for an ICD.
Incorrect: on its own, a rate-slowing drug risks lengthening post-conversion pauses and worsening syncope.
Correct: pacing is class I (ESC 2021); AF ablation (IIa) may avoid it in selected patients.
ecg-cond-020.explication: The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend pacing (class I) in the symptomatic tachycardia–bradycardia form of sinus node dysfunction, to correct the pauses and allow rate-slowing or antiarrhythmic treatment of AF, unless ablation of the tachyarrhythmia is preferred. AF ablation should be considered (class IIa) in selected patients to avoid implantation when the bradycardia is related to AF. Uptitrating the beta-blocker alone could worsen the pauses. An ICD has no role in the absence of ventricular arrhythmia. Observation alone is inappropriate after documented syncope.
ecg-cond-020.aRetenir: Symptomatic tachycardia–bradycardia: pacing (class I) or, in selected patients, AF ablation (IIa).

ecg-cond-021.question: Asymptomatic sinus bradycardia at 40 bpm during sleep warrants permanent pacing.
commentaires: Incorrect: asymptomatic sinus bradycardia, especially at night, is not an indication (class III, ESC 2021).
Correct: pacing is for bradycardia correlated with symptoms, not an isolated nocturnal rate; consider sleep apnoea.
ecg-cond-021.explication: False. Pacing is not recommended (class III, ESC 2021) in asymptomatic sinus node dysfunction or when bradycardia is due to a transient or reversible cause. Nocturnal rates of 35–40 bpm are common, particularly in young people or athletes, owing to vagal predominance. The key decision criterion in sinus node dysfunction is the correlation between symptoms and bradycardia, not an isolated heart rate value. Nocturnal bradycardia should, however, prompt a search for sleep apnoea syndrome.
ecg-cond-021.aRetenir: Sinus node dysfunction: pace bradycardia correlated with symptoms, not a heart rate number.

ecg-cond-022.question: Before accepting a pacing indication for bradycardia (sinus node dysfunction or AV block), which reversible or extrinsic causes should be sought?
commentaires: Correct: hypothyroidism slows sinus node automaticity and is a classic reversible cause.
Incorrect: hypokalaemia promotes ectopy and tachyarrhythmias; hyperkalaemia is what causes bradycardia and block.
Correct: the most common extrinsic cause, to be reassessed before any implantation (including beta-blocker eye drops).
Correct: sleep apnoea causes nocturnal bradycardia and pauses, often reversible with treatment.
Incorrect: hyperthyroidism causes sinus tachycardia or AF, not bradycardia.
ecg-cond-022.explication: The 2021 ESC guidelines stress the search for potentially reversible causes before any implantation: drugs (beta-blockers including eye drops, ivabradine, verapamil/diltiazem, digoxin, antiarrhythmic drugs), electrolyte disturbances (mainly hyperkalaemia), hypothyroidism, sleep apnoea, hypothermia, acute myocardial infarction and Lyme disease. Hypokalaemia rather promotes ectopic beats, tachyarrhythmias and torsades; it is hyperkalaemia that slows automaticity and conduction. Hyperthyroidism, by contrast, causes sinus tachycardia or AF, not bradycardia. Note, however, that if the rate-slowing drug is essential (e.g. a beta-blocker after myocardial infarction), symptomatic bradycardia may justify pacing without stopping the drug.
ecg-cond-022.aRetenir: Always exclude a reversible cause (drug, K+, thyroid, sleep apnoea, Lyme disease, ischaemia) before pacing.

ecg-cond-023.question: In a patient with suspected sinus node dysfunction who complains of exertional dyspnoea and fatigue, exercise testing is useful to look for chronotropic incompetence.
commentaires: Correct: exercise testing documents chronotropic incompetence, which the resting ECG and Holter monitoring can miss.
Incorrect: the statement is true; exercise allows dyspnoea to be correlated with an inadequate rate and guides rate response.
ecg-cond-023.explication: True. Chronotropic incompetence, i.e. the inability to increase heart rate appropriately during exercise, is a form of sinus node dysfunction that the resting ECG and Holter monitoring can miss. Exercise testing documents it and correlates breathlessness with an inadequate rate. It informs the choice of rate response (R mode) if a device is implanted. The result must be interpreted taking into account rate-slowing drugs and the level of exercise achieved.
ecg-cond-023.aRetenir: Exertional symptoms + suspected sinus node dysfunction: exercise test for chronotropic incompetence.

ecg-cond-024.question: Define tachycardia–bradycardia syndrome and explain why drug management is often difficult without pacing.
ecg-cond-024.reponseAttendue: A form of sinus node dysfunction combining atrial tachyarrhythmias (mainly AF/flutter) and bradycardia (sinus bradycardia, pauses, especially post-conversion pauses). The rate-slowing or antiarrhythmic drugs needed for the tachycardia worsen the bradycardia and pauses: pacing protects against bradycardia and allows these drugs to be used (alternatively: AF ablation in selected patients).
ecg-cond-024.explication: Tachycardia–bradycardia syndrome is a manifestation of sick sinus syndrome: diseased atrial tissue promotes AF and the diseased sinus node recovers poorly after episodes, hence pauses on termination that are sometimes syncopal. The therapeutic dilemma is classic: beta-blockers, digoxin or antiarrhythmic drugs control the tachycardia but worsen the pauses. The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend pacing (class I) to allow these treatments, unless ablation of the tachyarrhythmia is preferred; AF ablation should be considered (IIa) in selected patients to avoid implantation. Do not forget anticoagulation according to the thromboembolic risk score.
ecg-cond-024.aRetenir: Tachycardia–bradycardia: rate-slowing drugs worsen pauses, hence pacing or AF ablation.

ecg-cond-025.question: A 70-year-old asymptomatic man has this pre-operative ECG. What is the diagnosis?
options: Complete AV block with narrow escape
commentaires: Correct: constant PR interval of about 280 ms (> 200 ms), with every P wave conducted.
Incorrect: the PR interval measures about 7 small squares (≈ 280 ms), beyond the 200 ms limit.
Incorrect: every P wave is conducted with a fixed PR interval; no P wave is blocked.
Incorrect: the PR interval is constant and each P wave is followed by a QRS: there is no AV dissociation.
ecg-cond-025.explication: On this tracing, every P wave is conducted (1:1 ratio) with a constant PR interval of about 280 ms, above 200 ms: this is first-degree AV block, which is really just conduction delay rather than true "block". In Mobitz I, the PR interval would lengthen progressively until a P wave is blocked. Complete AV block would show dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes. The site is most often nodal, especially with narrow QRS complexes. Isolated and asymptomatic, it does not warrant pacing.
ecg-cond-025.aRetenir: First-degree AV block: PR > 200 ms, constant, every P wave conducted.

ecg-cond-026.question: In first-degree AV block, an isolated P wave may fail to conduct, provided the PR interval of the other beats remains above 200 ms.
commentaires: Incorrect: a single blocked sinus P wave is enough to define second-degree AV block, whatever the PR interval of the other beats.
Correct: first-degree AV block maintains 1:1 conduction; any blocked P wave means second-degree block.
ecg-cond-026.explication: False. First-degree AV block corresponds to prolonged AV conduction time (PR > 200 ms) without any blocked P wave: conduction remains 1:1. As soon as a single P wave is not conducted, this is second-degree AV block (Mobitz I, Mobitz II, 2:1 or high-grade), whatever the PR interval of the other beats. Beware of false blocked P waves: a blocked PAC, which is premature, does not constitute AV block. A very long PR interval (> 300 ms) may, however, cause atrial contraction against a closed mitral valve and symptoms resembling pacemaker syndrome.
ecg-cond-026.aRetenir: First-degree AV block = slowed 1:1 conduction; a single blocked sinus P wave means second-degree block.
